newsitem.title: UK: BAA says not losing hope for Heathrow T5.
newsitem.headline: BAA says not losing hope for Heathrow T5.

text.p: British airports operator BAA Plc denied on Friday that a change in accounting policy meant it now fears that its 1.5 billion pound project to build a giant fifth terminal at London Heathrow might be blocked by a planning inquiry.
The company said earlier that delays in completing the marathon inquiry had forced the company to stop capitalising interest on preparatory expenditure.
As a result it warned that it would book a 40 million pounds exceptional interest charge in its results for the year to March 31 1997 to write off the accumulated interest previously capitalised.

"It's not a lack of confidence on our part," finance director Russell Walls told Reuters. "It's just that with the delay this (capitalised interest) is becoming 30 percent of the total amount (spent) and it's compounding all the time."
"It's compounding on itself all the time and it's growing as a proportion faster than we are actually spending on the ground work (for the project)."

The company said that it would resume capitalising interest on the project if and when planning permission was granted, but it now does not expect to get planning permission until the turn of the century.
So far it has spent 178 million pounds on preparatory work, including site preparation, design work, and making its case at the planning inquiry, of which 49 million pounds was capitalised interest.
But it emphasised that only interest charges would be affected by the move, not the development costs themselves, which were currently running at around 30 million pounds a year.

"It just seemed to me that this was going on too long and with planning permission not now expected until the end of the century this interest was just going to roll up and roll up and roll up," said Walls.
"There would be too much capitalised interest sitting on this project," he added.

The public inquiry opened in May 1995 but fierce opposition led by environmental groups, local authorities and some residents means that the planning inspectorate does not expect to finish wading through submissions and hearing evidence until mid-1998.
Consequently BAA said on Friday that it did not now expect a government decision on the project until early in the year 2000.
"We reckon that the Inspector is likely to take a year to write his report and then the Secretaries of State for transport and environment have to make their decision between them," said Walls.
"If it took (another) six months for a decision that would be pretty good going," he said.
But it remains to be seen whether BAA could meet its revised schedule to open the first phase of the development in the year 2004, two years later than originally planned.
"If we get permission by the end of the century we can have the first phase open before the end of 2004," Walls said.

BAA announced on Thursday that it had agreed with British Airways that the British flag carrier and its alliance partners would get T5 and give up Terminal One to the alliance of United Airlines, Lufthansa, SAS, Air Canada and Thai Airways.

Last year, Heathrow handled nearly 56 million passengers but BAA and its airlines say the airport is now close to full capacity. T5 is designed to gradually increase capacity by 30 million passengers a year to over 80 million by the year 2013.
